title: Outside the Lab
text:
Outside the Lab
Way before I entered a research laboratory, I was already learning by building.
I began working on machines and engine projects during high school, initially out of curiosity and necessity. Over time, those ideas became increasingly ambitious, and in 2020, at age 20, that work developed into a business, initially logistics, and now solely focused on diesel systems, fabrication, and custom tow truck builds.
Although I enjoyed building a business and working with mechanical systems, I chose to continue pursuing science not only because I love it but also because I believe I have a lot to bring to science. Whether I am developing a piece of lab equipment, troubleshooting an experiment, or turning an idea for a truck into a functioning mechanism, I approach problems the same way, understand how the system works, identify what can be improved, and keep working until the idea becomes something real
These projects are a reminder of what I bring to research beyond my technical training, I take ownership of difficult problems, and do my best to carry ANY idea from concept through implementation

title: In the Lab
text:
In vivo: testing symbiotic performance
I evaluate selected strains using longitudinal plant symbiosis experiments in Medicago truncatula.
Plants are followed for approximately six weeks while I monitor the development of root nodules and changes in nodule phenotype over time.
Pink nodules provide a visible indicator associated with an effective symbiotic state, while white nodules can indicate nodules that have not fully developed or maintained that state.
At the end of the experiment, I measure leaf chlorophyll as an additional indicator of plant performance.



Comparison of a nodule photographed at week 4 and week 6 post inoculation

title: Denis Cruz - in the Chen Lab)
text:
I am an M.S. researcher at San Francisco State University studying how bacterial genetics shapes interactions between microbes and their hosts.
My current research uses the Sinorhizobium meliloti–Medicago symbiosis as a model to investigate how bacterial pathways involved in surface behavior, cellular regulation, and RNA organization influence host colonization and the maintenance of effective symbiosis.
Alongside my biological research, I draw on experience in engineering, fabrication, data analysis, and entrepreneurship. In my lab I constantly seek to develop practical tools and approaches that improve how our research is performed.

section: Approach at research and problem solving
text:
Approach at research and problem solving
All my work in and out the lab is driven my determination to understand the systems I work with, biological or not. Hard problems push us to generate better experiments, better tools, and eventually better technologies.


🧬 Research
Investigating genetic determinants of Sinorhizobium meliloti symbiotic performance in Medicago hosts, with particular interest in bacterial surface-associated behavior, regulatory pathways, and RNase E-dependent RNA organization.
Explore Research →


⚙️ Research Engineering
I enjoy designing and prototyping tools that address practical limitations in our experimental workflows. From custom 3D-printed lab components and devices for improving sample preparation and standardization to developing an in house seed-bulking workflow.
See Research Engineering →


🔧 Outside the Lab
My background in diesel systems, fabrication, and entrepreneurship shaped the way I approach scientific problems. I am interested in bringing that same problem-solving mindset into biotechnology and bioengineering.

title: engineering
text:
The problem
Plant symbiosis experiments are a big part of our research. Medicago–Sinorhizobium symbiosis experiments require plants to grow in transparent tubes while the developing root system stays protected from light.
For years our lab used aluminum foil molds. I found this difficult to use because it required repeated preparation and caution not to rip or fold the fragile paper. This also produced waste and allowed for variability in how completely each root zone was covered.



Before: Plant-growth tubes individually wrapped with aluminum foil.

title: engineering
text:
The solution
I designed reusable opaque sleeves that fit around our plant-growth tubes and provide consistent light protection that can be quickly removed and replaced during experimental observations.

After: Reusable 3D-printed sleeves implemented in the plant-growth system.

title: engineering
text:
The problem
Some microbiological procedures require Petri dishes to be divided into equal regions. Drawing these divisions manually can introduce small differences in positioning and requires repeated careful measurement for every plate.



Before: Manual plate division using repeated measurements and hand-drawn guides. Not consistent and slow and a problem when consistency is important in experimental workflows, such as CFU count verification.

title: engineering
text:
The solution
I designed reusable 3D-printed templates that align with the Petri dish and guide equal plate division.
This design includes reference features for multiple plate layouts, allowing the same tool to be used for different experimental configurations.

The template: Reusable 3D-printed template for consistently dividing Petri dishes.







In use: Six-section plate layout used to organize and streak multiple bacterial strains.

The problem
A structural component of a Thermo Scientific GENESYS spectrophotometer sample-compartment lid failed near the hinge assembly.
Rather than replacing the entire assembly, I reversed engineered, redesigned and fabricated the damaged component in house.

title: engineering
text:
The design process
I measured the original, reconstructed the component in CAD, and modified the design to accommodate the existing hinge and new hardware.
The redesign included changes to the walls, fastener placement and type, hinge alignment, and reinforcement around mechanically stressed regions.

title: engineering
text:
The problem
My symbiosis experiments require chlorophyll extraction from plant tissue as an endpoint measurement of plant performance.
Manual tissue disruption can be repetitive and may introduce variability in extraction efficiency between samples, particularly when processing larger experiments.

title: engineering
text:
Current development
I am developing a bead-based tissue disruption device intended to improve the speed and consistency of chlorophyll sample preparation.
The project is currently focused on designing a system that can process samples reproducibly while integrating with the existing extraction workflow.

text:
Research goal
Rather than changing the biological assay itself, the objective is to improve the sample processing step that precedes measurement.

Design goal: Increase throughput and standardize tissue disruption during chlorophyll extraction.

title: engineering
text:
The problem

The problem: aging seed stocks
Our existing Medicago truncatula seed lab-line stocks are more than 20 years old, cannot be bought and average about 2% germination. This creates a major bottleneck when preparing plants for symbiosis experiments.
Seeds aren’t just placed into incubation. Before germination, they undergo a multi-step sterilization and washing procedure that takes approximately 5–6 hours, followed by incubation and screening for contamination before seedlings can be used experimentally.
At a 2% germination rate, processing 1,500 seeds may yield only about 30 seedlings. Obtaining enough plants for a single symbiosis experiment can therefore require processing several thousand seeds, sometimes the equivalent of six or more 1,500 seed batches.
When germination is insufficient, additional batches must be prepared. This not only increases labor and material use, but can also result in seedlings germinating on different days, making it more difficult to establish a synchronized experimental cohort.These are from a special lab strain seed stock and cannot be bought.





Low germination of aged seed stock. Representative germination of Medicago truncatula seeds from a seed stock more than 20 years old.










NoteWhat 2% germination means



1,500 seeds processed → ~30 germinated seedlings
To obtain roughly 150–180 seedlings, thousands of seeds may need to be sterilized, washed, incubated, and screened for contamination.

title: engineering
text:
The approach
I developed an in-house seed-bulking workflow for M. truncatula and other experimental legumes. This has never been done in our lab and required me to learn about greenhouse plant production from the ground up. I had to learn about unfamiliar things such as substrate types, waterings, nutrition, light, and plant support. Our current plants are as healthy as they can be
This reflects an important part of how I approach research: when I encounter a problem outside my previous experience, I am willing to learn the system and refine the process until it works.






Early growth: Initial plants during the first stages of developing the greenhouse seed-bulking workflow.







Current : Large and robust plants following my greenhouse protocol for growing conditions and management.

title: engineering
text:
Research benefit
Developing an internal seed supply preserves access to our specialized Medicago truncatula Jemalong A17 line, which is not commercially available and provides a reliable source of experimental hosts for future symbiosis studies.
